q: A Climate Zone 6 (cold) project wants to maximize envelope performance per dollar spent. What investment has the best cost-to-performance ratio?
options: Improve the air barrier — leakage is 25–40% of heating loss in cold climates
Adding solar panels to supplement heating
Maximizing south-facing glazing for passive solar gain
Installing triple-pane windows on all south-facing glazing
purpose: Assess whether the learner can apply the EA concept and solve this best-fit question using the governing LEED v5 intent, scope, or requirement.
vocabulary: best: a word asking for the strongest or most effective option; energy and atmosphere: strategies addressing energy demand, efficiency, refrigerants, and renewable energy; energy efficiency: delivery of the required service with less energy use
keywords: Choose the option that addresses the stated LEED intent most directly, not a secondary benefit; decisive option: Improve the air barrier — leakage is 25–40% of heating loss in cold climates.
logic: In Climate Zone 6 cold climates, air leakage is often the dominant heating energy loss mechanism, accounting for 25–40% of heating energy loss. A comprehensive air barrier addresses this directly and tends to have the best cost-performance ratio compared to incremental insulation or window upgrades. It also improves comfort and moisture management.

q: A team discovers their zip code's 6 RP credits are all in categories they are not targeting. The team leader says 'let's pursue these RP credits just for the bonus points.' Is this correct?
options: Yes — RP credits can be pursued independently of the project's sustainability strategy
No — RP credits can only be earned if planned from project inception
Yes — RP credits are free points with no real requirements
Partially — credits can be pursued but only if they align with project goals and capability
purpose: Assess whether the learner can apply the PR concept and solve this exception question using the governing LEED v5 intent, scope, or requirement.
vocabulary: credit: an optional LEED requirement that can earn points; LEED: a third-party green building rating and certification system; compliance: satisfaction of the applicable requirement and documentation
keywords: Identify the exception or the option that does not satisfy the common LEED condition; decisive option: Partially — credits can be pursued but only if they align with project goals and capability.
logic: RP credits require earning the underlying base credit — they are not free points. While a team can certainly target RP-designated credits, pursuing credits that don't align with the project's design or operational context often wastes documentation effort. Strategic teams select RP credits that match their natural project strengths.

q: Site A is downtown near transit but requires $500K brownfield remediation. Site B is suburban, shovel-ready, no transit. Which provides better LEED value?
options: Site A is ineligible for LEED due to contamination history
Site B always wins because it is cheaper to develop
Site A — High Priority Site brownfield credit plus multiple transit and density credits
Both sites have identical LEED potential
purpose: Assess whether the learner can apply the LT concept and solve this concept question using the governing LEED v5 intent, scope, or requirement.
vocabulary: brownfield: previously developed land with actual or perceived contamination; credit: an optional LEED requirement that can earn points; location and transportation: strategies that reduce travel impacts through site selection and mobility options
keywords: Match the term, scope, or function in the question to the exact LEED concept; decisive answer: Site A — High Priority Site brownfield credit plus multiple transit and density credits.
logic: Location decisions have long-term consequences that often dwarf short-term remediation costs. A downtown transit-served building commands rent premiums, has lower parking costs, attracts talent, and earns significant LT credits. The $500K remediation cost is typically offset many times over by long-term property value premium.

q: Two flooring options: Option A is vinyl tile with HPD listing PVC and phthalates; Option B is linoleum with Declare label and no Red List chemicals. Which is LEED V5 preferred?
options: Both are equivalent since both have HPDs
Option B — Declare label and absence of Red List chemicals earns optimization credit
Option A earns more credit because PVC is a widely used material
Option A — VCT is more durable and cost-effective
purpose: Assess whether the learner can apply the MR concept and solve this concept question using the governing LEED v5 intent, scope, or requirement.
vocabulary: credit: an optional LEED requirement that can earn points; HPD: a Health Product Declaration reporting product ingredients and health information; materials and resources: strategies addressing life-cycle impacts, product selection, sourcing, and waste
keywords: Match the term, scope, or function in the question to the exact LEED concept; decisive answer: Option B — Declare label and absence of Red List chemicals earns optimization credit.
logic: Having an HPD discloses ingredients but does not mean the product meets ingredient optimization criteria. LEED rewards products that avoid Red List chemicals. PVC and phthalates are on the ILFI Red List. Option B's Declare certification confirming Red List compliance earns optimization credit; Option A's HPD disclosure of Red List chemicals disqualifies it.
